newsitem.title: UK: Hyder details preferences for windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: Hyder details preferences for windfall tax.

text.p: British multi-utility Hyder Plc would favour a method of calculation based on turnover or operating profit for a one-off tax on "excess profits" planned by the new Labour government, executives said on Monday.

"The simplest way would be based on published information and there is published information on turnover, operating profit, with reference to the regulated parts of the business," chief executive Graham Hawker told a press conference.
Hyder, which accepts the government has a mandate for such a tax, said in a statement with results that it sought "fairness and appropriateness in the basis of application of the levy".

Hawker said calculations based on turnover and operating profits would reflect the extent to which prices were fixed for utilities and the amount of customer rebates and extra investment which had been made.

He said Hyder would be disappointed if the government did not take into account voluntary rebates made to customers in the past and investments to improve services and the environment over and above agreed targets.
Chairman Iain Evans added Hyder would want any such tax to have a "breadth in application so no individual company was too badly hit".

The Labour government, which swept to power with a landslide majority on May 1, has vowed to make a one-off "windfall" tax to fund a three billion pound programme to cut unemployment a central plank of its first budget, due on July 2.
Further details are slim but companies were asked to submit comments to the Treasury by the end of May and regulators give their contributions in the first two weeks of June.
Hawker said Hyder would not want a tax based on total shareholder return because it would not reflect the company's concerns.
Hyder warned that if the tax were too onerous, it would have to look again at "our discretionary and environmental investments and voluntary customer discounts."
The company said it was spending an extra 40 million pounds in the next five years on investment in environmental areas such as improving beaches.
Hawker said the company would be "very loathe" to review this spending or voluntary customer rebates in the event of a punitive tax. -- London Newsroom +44171 542 7717
